Florence is a city of roofs, and almost nobody is ever above them.

The rooms that look out like this are on the top floor of buildings with no lift, which is why the load goes up in crates of twenty-five kilos and why the field kitchen is induction in pieces rather than gas. What reaches the top is exactly what one person could carry.

The view costs four flights. It is usually worth it.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Based in the city, cooking wherever the evening is.

Flame does not cook anything.

Embers cook, which means wood that has got to the end of itself, and for a hearth to be ready takes forty minutes in which nothing can go over it. Whoever is in a hurry cooks on the flame and sends out meat that is smoked on the outside and raw in the middle.

The fire is lit before the guests arrive, not with them.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. One event a day, cooked by hand, in rooms that are not venues.

Three doors open at once, and the room loses two degrees.

Which is the whole calculation. A room that opens onto a terrace is two rooms in one evening, and the moment you move between them is decided by the light rather than by the menu. We rehearse that changeover, and we never announce it.

The doors stay open until somebody asks for them to be closed.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. We arrive with the brigade and the field kitchen, and leave the room as we found it.

The centre of a table is the most expensive empty space in the room.

Whatever goes there has to be worth the two conversations it blocks, which is why it stays under fifteen centimetres and why there are no flowers in water: a vase is height, weight, and a spill waiting for somebody's elbow.

Low, or nothing at all.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Private dinners in Tuscan villas, cloisters and historic houses that have no kitchen of their own.

Three rooms in a line, and doors that have not been closed in a century.

An enfilade is a service problem disguised as a view. The distance from the last room to the kitchen is thirty metres, so the last room eats four minutes after the first unless you split the brigade and lose a pair of hands.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number seventeen.

Linen goes down damp and dries flat.

A cloth pressed in the morning and laid at six has a fold line in it by eight. Laid slightly damp, the fold disappears as the room warms. It is the oldest trick in the job and it costs nothing.

Brass is the opposite. Burnished once a season, then left alone.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. We lay the table, cook the dinner and leave the room as we found it.

Four square metres, and everything in them is fixed down.

A galley is not a small kitchen, it is a different kind of kitchen: no surface is free, so the work happens in sequence instead of side by side, and every step is decided before anyone comes aboard. Whatever can be done ashore is done ashore.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number eighteen.

You can hear a kitchen before you can see it.

At this hour there is one pot on and nothing else, and the sound is not a boil. A stock that boils goes cloudy and never comes back, so it is held just under, which in practice means somebody checks it every twenty minutes for eight hours.

The room smells of it long after it has been taken off.

The anteroom is the room nobody books and the one that saves every evening.

That is where the bar goes, that is where the coats end up, and that is where the guests spend the first forty minutes while the dining room stays shut. A room you see straight away is a room you have already seen.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number nineteen.

A dining room that has always been a dining room is the rarest thing on this list.

It comes with its own table, which is the catch: it cannot be moved, so the number of covers is decided by the furniture rather than by the client. Twenty-two, and the twenty-third sits in another room.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number twenty.

Deconsecrated, which is a legal fact and not an aesthetic one.

It changes what may be done here and it changes nothing about how the room behaves: stone floor, one high window, and several seconds of reverberation that make a seated dinner difficult and a standing reception excellent. We propose it for the second of those.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number twenty-one.

A window onto Florence is worth a course, and like a course it is served once.

If the guests walk in and find it open, ten minutes later they have stopped looking. The shutters stay closed until the second course and are opened while the table is cleared: it is the only moment of the evening when everybody stops talking at the same time.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number twenty-two.

A formal garden is a room whose walls are cut twice a year.

Nothing may be driven onto the gravel and nothing may be pegged into it, so everything free-standing is weighted instead, which is a heavier load in and a slower one out. In exchange there is no ceiling and no neighbour.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number twenty-three.

In a palazzo there is always a service stair, and it is behind a door that looks like a cupboard.

Finding it is the first thing we do on a site visit, before the kilowatts and before looking at the rooms. If there isn't one, the brigade goes where the guests go, and at that point you get to watch the evening being assembled.

That door appears in no photograph of the house. Which is why it appears here.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Everything comes in through one door and goes back out the same night.

Sixteen people, and the stairs decide everything.

A tower room is reached by one spiral flight, which means nothing goes up on wheels and nothing comes down while something else is going up. Service runs one way at a time, and plates are carried two at a time rather than four.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number twenty-four.

Five arches, and the valley does the rest.

The floor has never been level here, because it was laid to shed rain, so every table is shimmed before anything goes on it and the trolleys are chocked. Thirty covers, one row along the arches, and the last two metres stay clear because that is where the wind comes in.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number twenty-five.
